mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states she never went back for follow-up glucose testing after her gestational diabetes pregnancy and implies no one really explained why it mattered
mismatches.recordEvidence: The 4-year-old OB note documents that she was explicitly advised of lifetime type 2 diabetes risk and told to have screening every 1-3 years, with no follow-up screening visit found in the chart since
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may not retain or fully process risk counseling given during an acute pregnancy-related visit; this is an opportunity to re-explain gestational diabetes as a strong risk factor and to close the counseling loop in a way that sticks, rather than assuming the earlier advice failed to happen.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient describes her recent yeast infection as treated and attributes recurrence simply to bad luck, not connecting it to blood sugar
mismatches.recordEvidence: The urgent care note explicitly documents that recurrent yeast infections can be associated with uncontrolled blood sugar and that no glucose testing was performed at that visit, despite this being a known association
mismatches.teachingPoint: Recurrent candidiasis in an adult woman should prompt consideration of undiagnosed diabetes; this visit is the first time the connection is being made explicit for the patient, highlighting a missed screening opportunity at a prior encounter.

objectives.text: Correctly interpret HbA1c and fasting glucose results to diagnose type 2 diabetes mellitus and explain the diagnosis in plain language connecting it to her symptoms (thirst, fatigue, recurrent yeast infections)

answerKey.primaryProblem: Newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.6%, fasting glucose 178 mg/dL) in a 38-year-old woman with prior gestational diabetes, strong family history, obesity, and dyslipidemia
differential: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (confirmed by two abnormal measures: HbA1c and fasting glucose)
Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA) - less likely given age, BMI, and gradual symptom onset, but consider if poor response to oral therapy or unexpected insulin requirement develops
Secondary causes of hyperglycemia (e.g., medication-induced, Cushing syndrome) - no supporting history
Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis from other causes (e.g., antibiotic use, immunosuppression) - less likely; most consistent with underlying hyperglycemia
keyFindings: HbA1c 8.6% and fasting glucose 178 mg/dL, both diagnostic of diabetes
History of gestational diabetes 4 years ago with no interval screening since
Strong family history of diabetes with end-stage renal disease on dialysis (mother) and amputation (uncle)
Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis as a presenting symptom of hyperglycemia
LDL 142 mg/dL and triglycerides 165 mg/dL indicating need for cardiovascular risk reduction
UACR 22 mg/g, within normal range but near upper threshold, warranting repeat testing to establish trend
BMI 34 (obesity) and acanthosis nigricans supporting insulin resistance
Significant fear of insulin/dialysis and informational overwhelm shaping treatment preferences
plan: Explain diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus in plain language, explicitly linking it to her thirst, fatigue, and recurrent yeast infections

Initiate metformin 500 mg orally once daily with meals, with plan to titrate up over several weeks as tolerated to reduce GI side effects, explaining mechanism and that this is a pill, not an injection
Order repeat UACR in 3-6 months and continue annual monitoring given value near upper limit of normal
Discuss statin therapy consideration given LDL 142 and diabetes diagnosis per guideline-based cardiovascular risk reduction; coordinate initiation per practice protocol
Refer for dilated eye exam (diabetic retinopathy screening) and for comprehensive foot exam/podiatry if any future abnormal findings

Set collaborative, shift-work-sensitive goals: swap sweetened tea/energy drinks for water or unsweetened alternatives during shifts, aim for a 10-minute walk on most days, and plan simple, lower-carbohydrate options for convenience meals
Recommend diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES) referral and connect with a dietitian familiar with shift-work schedules
Address missed interval screening after gestational diabetes by closing the loop: schedule reliable annual follow-up and document clearly in the plan
Update immunizations: recommend pneumococcal vaccination given diabetes diagnosis; discuss hepatitis B vaccination per diabetes-specific recommendations

Address recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis: if symptoms persist or recur after glycemic improvement, consider referral for STI testing/evaluation if not already done, and treat as needed within scope; reassess once glucose is better controlled

Screen for diabetes distress and provide emotional support; validate fear of needles/dialysis while clarifying that oral therapy and lifestyle change are the appropriate first step at this stage, not a sign that injections are imminent
Schedule follow-up visit in 4-6 weeks to assess metformin tolerance, repeat fasting glucose, and reinforce self-management goals
redFlags: Symptoms of diabetic ketoacidosis (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, confusion) would require urgent/emergency referral, not managed in this visit
Signs of severe or worsening infection, vision loss, or chest pain/shortness of breath would require escalation beyond routine primary care follow-up
If UACR trends upward into the microalbuminuria range on repeat testing, or eGFR declines, nephrology referral should be considered rather than managed solely in primary care
Significant depressive symptoms or suicidal ideation, if present, would require mental health referral beyond this visit's scope
educationPoints: Gestational diabetes is a strong risk factor for later type 2 diabetes, and guidelines recommend ongoing screening every 1-3 years after pregnancy, not a one-time check
Recurrent vaginal yeast infections in an adult can be a presenting sign of undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes due to glucose-rich tissue environments favoring fungal growth

Metformin is an oral medication, not an injection, and is first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes; starting it promptly at diagnosis (alongside lifestyle change) is standard practice, not a sign of worsening disease

Realistic, culturally and contextually tailored goals (e.g., swapping sweetened beverages, brief walks around a rotating shift schedule) are more sustainable and effective than generic diet/exercise advice

Family history of diabetes complications (dialysis, amputation) can be a strong motivator but also a source of fear; acknowledging this fear directly while clarifying the current treatment stage helps build trust and adherence
Diabetes diagnosis warrants a broader preventive care review, including lipid management, kidney function monitoring, eye and foot screening, and selected vaccinations

patient.name: Shanelle Robinson
patient.appearance: A woman in her late 30s with shoulder-length braided hair, wearing a company polo shirt, seated at a kitchen table with a calendar and children's school papers visible in the background. She appears tired but engaged, occasionally glancing off-screen as if listening for her children, and her affect shifts between anxious and attentive.

persona.personality: Practical, protective of her children, and quietly anxious beneath a composed, no-nonsense exterior
persona.communicationStyle: Direct and conversational, asks clarifying questions when confused, sometimes talks quickly when nervous
persona.emotionalState: Overwhelmed and frightened about long-term complications, but motivated to take action if given clear, practical guidance
persona.background: Shanelle has worked at the same call center for 9 years, recently promoted to supervisor, and manages rotating day/night shifts. She is raising three children (ages 6, 10, and 14) mostly on her own, with occasional help from her sister. She enjoys watching reality TV with her kids on days off and used to sing in her church choir before her schedule made it hard to attend regularly.
speechExamples: I just want somebody to give me a straight answer instead of all these different things I'm reading online.
I'm not trying to end up like my mother, on that machine three times a week.
Can you just tell me plain what I need to do, because I've got about ten minutes before I need to go get my kids.
I'll do the pills if I have to, I just really don't want shots.
concerns: Fear of eventually needing insulin injections or dialysis like her mother
Affordability of medications and healthier food on a limited budget
Confusion from conflicting diabetes information found online
Finding realistic ways to manage diet and activity around a rotating shift schedule

scenario.studentBrief: You are seeing Shanelle Robinson, a 38-year-old call-center supervisor, for a telehealth follow-up visit to discuss recent lab results after she reported thirst, fatigue, and recurrent yeast infections. She has a history of gestational diabetes and a strong family history of diabetes complications. Review her labs, explain the diagnosis, and develop an initial management plan within your scope as a nurse practitioner.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up to discuss lab results after reporting thirst, fatigue, and recurrent yeast infections
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thanks for seeing me. I'm here to go over my blood work. The nurse said my sugar came back high and I've been so thirsty and tired, plus I keep getting these yeast infections.
tasks: Explain the new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus in a way that connects to her reported symptoms
Initiate first-line pharmacologic therapy (metformin) and address her fear of injections
Negotiate realistic, shift-work-sensitive self-management goals around diet, sweetened beverages, and activity
Develop a screening, monitoring, and vaccination plan (lipids, kidney function, eye/foot exam, immunizations)
Address the gap in follow-up since her gestational diabetes diagnosis and provide emotional support for her fear of complications

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home at her kitchen table in Charlotte, NC, on a break between caregiving tasks
profile.summary: A 38-year-old call-center supervisor with a history of gestational diabetes and a strong family history of diabetes complications presents by telehealth to review labs confirming new type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.6%). The case teaches diagnosis communication, first-line metformin initiation, context-sensitive goal-setting for shift workers, and a comprehensive screening/vaccination plan, while highlighting a missed prior screening opportunity and the diagnostic significance of recurrent candidiasis.
profile.title: New Type 2 Diabetes Diagnosis in a Shift-Working Mother with Prior Gestational Diabetes
